42867719.text: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is a tumor with a dismal prognosis, as the majority of patients are diagnosed when the tumor is not resectable. Neoadjuvant treatment has significantly improved prognosis, but assessing treatment response can be challenging for radiologists. Given the fibrotic nature of the primary tumor, differentiating between residual viable tumor and fibrotic response can be difficult. MRI can have a role in reassessing the primary tumor and disease spread. In this review, we discuss MR techniques that can be used for this assessment, including routinely used sequences (e.g., DWI) and sequences that are not yet routinely included in pancreatic protocols (e.g., T1 mapping, ECV imaging, and USPIO contrast for nodal staging). KEY POINTS: Question Imaging assessment of the response of pancreatic adenocarcinoma to neoadjuvant treatment is difficult and still has limited accuracy. Findings Different MRI sequences and techniques have been suggested as possibly improving this assessment, reflecting on better patient management. Critical relevance statement We summarize the available evidence on MRI for restaging pancreatic carcinoma after neoadjuvant treatment.

42912569.text: 99m Tc sulphur colloid lymphoscintigraphy scan is a safe, noninvasive technique for the visualization of lymphatic pathways in the body. While primarily used to detect lymphatic obstruction, it is also valuable in identifying lymphatic extravasation, guiding targeted treatment strategies. We report a 33-year-old woman who developed a large pelvic fluid collection following renal transplantation, initially misdiagnosed on CT. Dynamic lymphoscintigraphy combined with SPECT/CT accurately identified the etiology and precise anatomic origin of the collection, guiding successful conservative management. This case highlights the complementary role of dynamic lymphoscintigraphy and SPECT/CT in diagnosing unexpected post-transplant complications, where conventional imaging alone may be misleading.

42951719.text: Companion animals occupy an increasingly important clinical and societal space, with dogs and cats often managed as family members and receiving advanced diagnostic and therapeutic care. Many veterinary nuclear medicine procedures are adapted from human practice, while naturally occurring canine and feline diseases provide opportunities for comparative and translational insight. This review mapped and synthesised the literature on nuclear medicine imaging and radionuclide therapy in dogs and cats, with emphasis on clinically mature applications and relevance to human nuclear medicine. A PRISMA-aligned systematic evidence map with focused narrative synthesis were undertaken. MEDLINE via PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection were searched, with supplementary Google Scholar searching, reference-list screening and citation mining. Because of heterogeneity in species, indication, radiopharmaceutical, protocol, comparator and outcome reporting, formal meta-analysis was not performed. A total of 228 articles were included. The literature was predominantly imaging-focused, with 176 articles addressing imaging alone, 34 therapy alone and 18 both imaging and therapy. Feline nuclear medicine was dominated by thyroid disease, particularly thyroid scintigraphy and radioiodine therapy for hyperthyroidism. Canine nuclear medicine was broader, including oncology PET/CT, osteosarcoma imaging and therapy, renal and hepatobiliary functional scintigraphy, portosystemic shunt imaging, neurology/behavioural imaging, thyroid carcinoma and radiosynoviorthesis. PET/CT was most prominent in canine oncology, while conventional scintigraphy remained important where functional information could not be replaced by structural imaging. Companion animal nuclear medicine is clinically useful and translationally relevant. Its most mature model is feline thyroid scintigraphy and radioiodine therapy, while its most dynamic future directions lie in canine oncology, molecular imaging and radiotheranostics. Closer collaboration between veterinary specialists and human nuclear medicine professionals may improve companion animal care while informing broader development of molecular imaging and targeted radionuclide therapy.

42972169.text: Foodborne illness affects an estimated 48 million people in the United States each year, and outbreaks peak in the summer. Recalls during the summer of 2026 involved eggs, jalapeños, and frozen blueberries, along with a Cyclospora outbreak traced to iceberg lettuce that caused more than 12,000 illnesses and over 550 hospitalizations. Furthermore, they caused nationwide public anxiety and dominated news headlines. Patients with enteric infection usually reach the emergency department with abdominal pain, and radiologists often read their CT before stool studies return or before anyone suspects infection. This review describes the CT findings of bacterial and parasitic enteritis and colitis. Common features include symmetric segmental or diffuse bowel wall thickening with submucosal edema, mucosal hyperenhancement producing a halo or target pattern, associated fat stranding, engorged mesenteric vessels, and lymphadenopathy. CT also shows complications including toxic megacolon, perforation, and abscess. Recognition of these findings supports timely diagnosis and appropriate management of infectious enterocolitis.

43002569.text: A 66-year-old woman with left upper abdominal pain had a solitary splenic mass nearly inconspicuous on unenhanced CT but progressively enhancing, although hypoattenuating relative to adjacent splenic parenchyma, on contrast-enhanced CT. 18F-FDG PET/CT showed intense uptake (SUVmax, 15.1) without additional suspicious hypermetabolic foci within the imaged field of view. CT suggested a potentially malignant splenic neoplasm, with lymphoma among the preoperative considerations. Splenectomy confirmed Rosai-Dorfman disease. No recurrence was identified on CT at 10 months. This case illustrates the broad differential diagnosis of solitary FDG-avid splenic masses.

43020619.text: Liver biopsy remains the gold standard for fibrosis assessment; however, its invasiveness limits its suitability for routine clinical use. The rising prevalence of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) as a leading cause of chronic liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma underscores the need for reliable noninvasive assessment. Current noninvasive imaging methods provide surrogate measures of fibrosis but do not directly assess fibrogenic activity. In contrast, fibroblast activation protein inhibitor (FAPI) PET enables molecular imaging of activated fibroblasts, a key driver of fibrosis. This study evaluates dynamic 18F-FAPI-74 PET imaging to assess hepatic fibrogenic activity in MASLD. Methods: In this prospective pilot study, 10 subjects (3 healthy volunteers, 4 patients with mild-moderate fibrosis, and 3 patients with advanced fibrosis) underwent 60-min dynamic 18F-FAPI-74 PET/CT. SUV and blood-normalized SUV ratio (SUVR) were quantified across time frames, and the net influx rate was derived from dynamic data. MR elastography-derived liver stiffness values were obtained for comparison. Correlations with histologic fibrosis scoring of biopsy tissue were assessed using Spearman analysis. Results: At 5 min postinjection, SUVR correlated strongly with histologic fibrosis score (ρ = 0.95; 95% CI, 0.75-1.00; P = 1.89 × 10-5), followed by SUV (ρ = 0.78; 95% CI, 0.23-0.98; P = 0.0077) and net influx rate from kinetic modeling (ρ = 0.84; 95% CI, 0.41-0.98; P = 0.0022). SUVR at the 4- to 5-min interval allowed clearer differentiation among healthy volunteers, patients with mild fibrosis, and patients with advanced fibrosis. Conclusion: Dynamic 18F-FAPI-74 PET enables quantitative visualization of hepatic fibroblast activation in MASLD. SUVR at the 4- to 5-min interval correlates more strongly with fibrosis severity, supporting 18F-FAPI-74 PET as a promising molecular biomarker for assessing and potentially monitoring metabolic fibrosis.

43084169.label: Objectives
43084169.text: To characterize radiology residents' training experience and reporting practices in rectal MRI staging in Romania, an Eastern European training environment.

43084169.label: Materials and methods
43084169.text: A multicenter, cross-sectional survey with nationwide dissemination was conducted in late 2025. A pretested questionnaire developed by a three-member panel was distributed through the Romanian Society of Radiology and Medical Imaging and residency coordinators. Items addressed demographics, rectal MRI exposure, self-assessed difficulty and confidence, practice context, learning methods, and structured reporting. Spearman's rank correlation assessed the association between residency year and self-reported rectal MRI exposure.

43084169.label: Results
43084169.text: Of 160 respondents (estimated survey uptake: 16.0%, 24.7%, or 23.4%, depending on denominator), 142 with prior general MRI experience formed the main analytic cohort. Higher residency year was associated with greater reported rectal MRI exposure (Spearman's rho = 0.527, p < 0.001), although exposure remained limited: approximately 70% of fifth-year residents reported ≤ 30 cases. Confidence was lowest for T4a and EMVI. Practice-context barriers included limited case volume (33.1%) and restricted resident involvement in interpretation (9.2-11.3%). Internet-based platforms (90.1%) and peer-to-peer learning (57.7%) were the dominant learning methods; only 10.6% attended dedicated workshops. Local training activities were rated useful or very useful by 87.3% of respondents. Prior use of structured reporting for rectal MRI was reported by 21.8%.

43084169.label: Conclusions
43084169.text: This multicenter survey suggests a potential training gap in rectal MRI staging during radiology residency in Romania. Reported exposure remained limited even in later residency years, learning was predominantly self-directed, and a minority of respondents reported prior use of structured reporting.

43084169.label: Key points
43084169.text: Question Rectal MRI staging is complex and clinically important, but residents' actual exposure, learning pathways, and structured reporting use during training remain poorly described. Findings A Romanian multicenter survey identified limited rectal MRI exposure, variable confidence across staging tasks, and prior structured reporting use among 21.8% of respondents. Critical relevance statement Identifying limited resident exposure, self-directed learning, and limited prior use of structured reporting supports targeted residency training and more consistent rectal MRI staging practice.

43102569.label: Objective
43102569.text: To determine whether nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM) degeneration and glymphatic dysfunction act independently or interactively associated with medial temporal tau vulnerability and cognitive impairment across the Alzheimer's disease (AD) continuum.

43102569.label: Methods
43102569.text: In this cross-sectional study, 114 participants, including 23 amyloid-negative normal controls (NC), 55 amyloid-positive individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 36 amyloid-positive patients with AD, underwent amyloid (Aβ) PET/CT and tau PET/MR scans. Glymphatic function was quantified with diffusion tensor imaging along perivascular spaces (DTI-ALPS) index and centrum semiovale perivascular space volume fraction (PVSVF-CSO). A perivascular imaging composite (PIC), derived from the reverse-coded ALPS index and PVSVF-CSO, was further used to evaluate its interaction effects with normalized NBM volume on medial temporal tau burden. Elastic net regression was used to examine multimodal prediction of cognitive performance.

43102569.label: Results
43102569.text: Normalized NBM volume and ALPS index progressively decreased across the AD continuum (all P < 0.05), PVSVF-CSO was higher in the MCI and AD groups than in the NC group (adjusted P = 0.005 and 0.003, respectively). In the combined symptomatic cohort, smaller normalized NBM volume and lower ALPS index were associated with higher selected medial temporal regions tau burden and worse cognitive performance (all P < 0.05). Parahippocampal gyrus (PHG) tau partially mediated the association between normalized NBM volume and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score (indirect effect: β = 17.25, 95% CI [0.52, 34.04], accounted for 27.9% of the total effect). Normalized NBM volume and its interaction with PIC were significantly associated with PHG tau burden (β = - 0.394, P < 0.001; β = - 0.166, P = 0.042). The exploratory elastic net model modestly predicted MoCA score (R2 = 0.105).

43102569.label: Conclusions
43102569.text: Cholinergic degeneration and glymphatic dysfunction are interrelated processes that show an interactive association with selected medial temporal tau vulnerability. PHG tau partially mediates the association between normalized NBM volume and cognitive performance.
